question: Which earlier idea, rather than the famous main tune, crowns the ending?
intro: A C-minor introduction gives way to a horn call, a brass chorale and the broad C-major tune that invited comparison with Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy”. Keep those three ideas distinct: their different returns shape the finale’s argument.

sections.label: Introduction · Adagio in C minor
sections.mNote: sustained phrases alternate with accelerating plucked strings

sections.label: Più andante · the horn call
sections.mNote: a new C-major perspective before the main Allegro

sections.label: Chorale and preparation
sections.mNote: low-brass chords precede the renewed horn-call preparation

sections.label: Allegro · the broad string tune
sections.mNote: main tune leads to the contrasting second group

cues.title: A descending beginning
cues.text: Low strings begin with a descending line, and the orchestra unfolds a slow C-minor phrase above it. The finale does not begin with the broad major-key tune: it first exposes fragments and the descending shape that will continue beneath later themes.
cues.evidence: Simrock p. 43 shows the low-string descent and overlapping slow orchestral phrase. The report rises from its quiet opening into a swell around 0:05, then recedes through 0:30; the note describes the initial passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Plucked notes gather momentum
cues.text: In the introduction’s plucked-string passages, short figures pass between orchestral registers and gain momentum. Compare those separated attacks with the sustained phrases around them: Brahms makes interruption part of the introduction’s design.
cues.evidence: The score’s first pizzicato passage begins at bar 6, visible on p. 43. Strong boundaries at 0:36 and 0:40 follow the low-level 0:25–0:30 stretch and accompany more detected attacks; this is passage placement, not an aligned accelerando.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Continuity through interruption
cues.text: Across the introduction, hear the long phrases and the plucked interruptions as contrasting uses of the same string body. The abrupt changes in articulation keep a steady lyrical flow from becoming established too soon.
cues.evidence: The score alternates sustained writing with pizzicato passages at bars 6–11 and 16–19. The report has another low-level span around 1:05–1:15 and changes at 1:18 and 1:32; no exact bow-change time is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The minor opening presses forward
cues.text: The introduction gathers weight again before changing its pace and colour. Listen through the rise and withdrawal, rather than expecting one uninterrupted crescendo to deliver the main tune.
cues.evidence: The report rises around 1:30–1:40, retreats at 1:45–1:50, and rises again at 1:55–2:00 before the 2:10 boundary. These measured changes support the alternating contour, not specific instrument entrances.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A greeting sent to Clara
cues.text: In 1868 Brahms sent Clara Schumann a precursor of the finale’s horn melody from the Bernese Alps as a birthday greeting. The private message predates the completed symphony; it does not establish a literal story for every passage around the call.
cues.evidence: Malte Krasting’s Berliner Philharmoniker note documents the 1868 greeting and its relation to the alphorn theme: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor-op-68/. The restriction against a literal programme is editorial caution.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A call above tremolo
cues.text: The Più andante section gives the horn call a background of softly moving string tremolo; flute later carries the melody. Listen for the long wind line against the rapid repeated bow strokes, rather than confusing those strokes with a faster melody.
cues.evidence: The score introduces the horn call at bar 30, p. 48, and passes it to flutes from bar 38. The 2:10 boundary leads to a steadier C-centred stretch through 3:20; flute timing is left approximate within that section.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chorale held in reserve
cues.text: Before the Allegro, trombones and bassoons present a compact chorale in chordal phrases. Keep its outline separate from the horn call: this quieter idea, rather than a new theme, will supply the final coda’s enlarged brass statement.
cues.evidence: Bars 47–51 contain the chorale, and bar 407 brings its expanded return. The strong 3:28 boundary and reduced brightness through 3:45 support approximate placement in this stretch; the chorale’s first chord is not precisely aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Allegro waits for space
cues.text: The preparation for the main tune recedes onto a held dominant harmony. The ensuing Allegro begins with a string melody over plucked lower strings, not with the full brass force that the finale will eventually reach.
cues.evidence: The score’s preparation ends before the Allegro at bar 62, p. 52. The report reaches its lowest internal level at 4:30 and changes strongly at 4:34, supporting the approximate 274-second Allegro boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Beethoven’s recognisable neighbour
cues.text: The broad C-major string tune resembles the “Ode to Joy” theme of Beethoven’s Ninth. When the resemblance was pointed out, Brahms is reported to have replied, “Any ass can see that”. Resemblance is the claim here, not a note-for-note quotation.
cues.evidence: Cross-checked with the documented influence edge beethoven-9-finale--brahms-1-finale-theme in content/influence/romantic.json. Mandel discusses the melodic resemblance and reported reply: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor. The reply is retained as reported speech, not a surviving first-hand transcript.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A broad tune becomes active material
cues.text: The Allegro’s first melody need not remain a complete song. Its opening turn can be detached and driven onwards through heavier scoring, so the tune supplies both a long phrase and short figures for transition.
cues.evidence: From bar 94 the score fragments the main theme into a more active transition. The report rises through 5:30–5:45 after the initial lower-level statements; this anchors the approximate transition region, not a specific turn figure.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remember the earlier horn call
cues.text: Throughout the Allegro, keep the introduction’s horn melody in mind as well as the broad string tune. Fragments of the call can connect different sections; the slow introduction has supplied working material, not just an opening atmosphere.
cues.evidence: The score recalls the horn theme in the transition from bar 114 and again during the later developmental span. This is a movement-wide comparison; no single horn entrance is assigned to 6:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A descending bass has a memory
cues.text: The second group sets melodic motion above a repeating four-note descent in the bass. That descending shape reaches back to the movement’s opening. Follow the lower line as a source of continuity when the upper melody changes.
cues.evidence: The score introduces the second group and its descending bass at bar 118, with a continuation at bar 132. The lower-level region around 6:20–7:05 follows the earlier transition crest; the note covers the group rather than its first bass statement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing material rises and retreats
cues.text: The exposition’s later material alternates growing weight with more exposed phrases. Listen for the persistence of the small rhythmic figures through those changes; an orchestral retreat is not necessarily a new formal beginning.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −27.0 dB at 7:05 to −9.1 at 7:20, falls at 7:30–7:45 and rises again at 7:50–8:00. The wording follows the measured contour without naming a precise cadence.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A cadence opens another question
cues.text: After the exposition’s forceful closing gestures, listen for the main tune to regain the foreground. Its return is not the end of the movement’s harmonic exploration; Brahms places more development inside the returning material.
cues.evidence: The score closes the exposition before the main theme returns at bar 186. The report withdraws at 8:20 and recovers at 8:25; these features support the approximate 505-second return rather than a rigid development–recapitulation division.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return and development overlap
cues.text: The broad tune returns with a fuller accompaniment, but its continuation moves away again. Listen for recognition and instability together: the familiar melody does not guarantee that the harmony will remain at home.
cues.evidence: Bars 186–219 restate the main theme and then divert its continuation towards E♭ and F♯. The report’s 8:25–8:45 C-centred stretch changes to E♭ around 8:55–9:00, with strong later boundaries at 9:02 and 9:14; the score supplies the tonal reading.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The transition returns with force
cues.text: The argument gathers weight after the returning tune’s quieter diversions. Familiar turning figures and descending motion become active again; compare this renewed push with the first transition out of the broad melody.
cues.evidence: The score restates transition material at bar 220 before further development. A strong boundary at 9:28 follows the level rise from −23.7 dB at 9:20 to −10.7 at 9:25; it supports the approximate renewed transition.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Scales are not empty filling
cues.text: Across the developmental passages, descending string scales continue under short wind figures. Listen to their direction and the way they are handed between registers: accompaniment can carry the motion even when the theme has been reduced to fragments.
cues.evidence: Bars 232–267 develop descending scales and the main tune’s turning figure, described in Hansen’s score guide. This general listening point does not assign a particular scale to 10:08.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The first score appeared in 1877
cues.text: The first orchestral score was published by Simrock in October 1877, after the 1876 premiere. The Brahms-Institut’s copy came from Theodor Kirchner’s estate; its scanned pages preserve the first edition used for this guide’s orchestral descriptions.
cues.evidence: The Brahms-Institut catalogue gives the publication month, plate 7957 and Kirchner provenance: https://brahmsinstitut.de/Archiv/web/bihl_digital/jb_werkekatalog/op_068.html. This does not identify the modern performers’ edition.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Pressure accumulates in the middle
cues.text: The central argument sustains a heavier orchestral stretch before another withdrawal. Keep following the descending and turning figures inside it: the buildup enlarges familiar gestures rather than announcing a separate melody.
cues.evidence: The report maintains elevated relative level from 10:35 through 11:35, then drops after the 11:38 boundary. The score’s developmental span combines those recurring shapes, but their individual attacks are not aligned.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The call has another setting
cues.text: When the horn melody returns later in the finale, the strings no longer simply provide the introduction’s tremolo background. Smoother moving harmony changes its surroundings. Compare the call’s melodic identity with the different texture carrying it.
cues.evidence: Hansen’s description of bars 289–300 distinguishes the returning horn melody’s moving strings from the introduction’s tremolo. The report’s lower-level span after 11:38 is compatible with that broader return region, but its first note is not fixed here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Space before the later second group
cues.text: A gradual withdrawal opens room for the next part of the argument. Listen across the quieter stretch for continuity in the lower lines; reduced volume does not erase the harmonic direction towards the home key.
cues.evidence: Relative level decreases from −7.6 dB at 12:10 to −25.8 at 12:50 before the 12:54 boundary. This is a measured retreat; the report’s key estimates are not published as chord labels.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The descending group comes home
cues.text: The later second group brings its descending bass pattern into C-major surroundings. The descending figure is redistributed between winds and lower strings, so a returning harmonic idea also becomes an exchange of orchestral colours.
cues.evidence: Bars 301–325 return the second group in C and alternate its descending figure between winds and low strings. The 12:54 boundary and rise in brightness through 13:00–13:20 support the approximate 774-second sectional anchor.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C major is not yet permanent
cues.text: The later closing material turns back towards C minor before the final major-key ending. Listen for that renewed minor colouring as part of the design: the first appearance of the broad C-major tune did not settle the entire finale.
cues.evidence: The score places the later closing group in C minor from bar 326. The report’s minor-compatible region around 13:35–14:00 follows the brighter second-group span; this confirms a broad score-based reading, not exact chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The symphony crosses the Atlantic
cues.text: Leopold Damrosch conducted the first American performance in New York’s Steinway Hall on 15 December 1877. The work reached Boston the following month, when Carl Zerrahn conducted it at the Music Hall.
cues.evidence: The Boston Symphony performance-history note gives New York, 15 December 1877, and Boston, 3 January 1878: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The final buildup begins quietly
cues.text: The final span starts from reduced weight and accumulates pressure again. Shorter fragments, repeated figures and increasing motion prepare the faster coda; the ending is built from another ascent rather than attached as an isolated fanfare.
cues.evidence: Bars 367–390 prepare the Più allegro with fragmenting material and stringendo. The report’s 14:48 boundary precedes a rise from −20.4 dB at 14:50 to −6.9 at 15:20; the precise tempo-change bar is not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chorale takes the larger role
cues.text: In the final coda, the chorale first heard quietly before the Allegro returns in expanded orchestral force. The famous broad tune is not simply repeated to crown the ending: an earlier, more compact idea acquires the greater weight.
cues.evidence: Bar 407 restores the chorale from bars 47–51. The report places sustained high relative level across the final span, including 15:25–15:30 and 15:55; this broad coda placement is not an aligned first brass chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C major under sustained pressure
cues.text: The closing passage keeps its C-major destination while short figures continue to drive forwards. Listen for the bass and the repeated orchestral chords working together: the final key is established before the last sound has finished.
cues.evidence: The score’s final bars 447–457 confirm C major through repeated orchestral chords and a timpani-supported close. The report remains broadly C-centred and high-level through 16:40, with a final renewed crest at 16:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chord and its resonance
cues.text: The last orchestral statement is followed by a short decay, not an extended quiet coda. Keep listening after the attack: the final resonance completes the contrast with the slow, interrupted beginning.
cues.evidence: Relative level moves from −6.6 dB at 16:50 to −39.4 at 16:55 before the 1016.9-second file ends. The report anchors the final decay, not an exact note-off time.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: The minor surge yields to a call
transitions.how: The Adagio’s surging strings and wind descents reach a forceful interruption, then withdraw. At Più andante the harmony turns to C major, the horn melody extends over a soft timpani roll, and muted upper strings provide tremolo. Trombones join the symphony’s orchestral palette here. A long-breathed line replaces the introduction’s broken alternation of sustained and plucked gestures.
transitions.evidence: The first-edition score p. 48, bar 30, shows Più andante, the horn call, trombones, timpani and con sordini strings. The strong 2:10 boundary follows the 1:55–2:00 crest; timing remains approximate.

transitions.title: A flowing call becomes chordal speech
transitions.how: After horn and flute have extended the call, trombones and bassoons present a short chorale with a much more chordal texture. Its grouped phrases interrupt the sense of a continuous solo line. The horn-call material subsequently resumes and builds towards the held dominant that prepares the Allegro; the chorale is therefore set aside as a distinct idea to be recovered in the final coda.
transitions.evidence: The score places the chorale at bars 47–51 and the renewed call from bar 52. The report’s 3:28 boundary accompanies lower brightness through 3:45; 208 seconds locates the broad change, not the first chord.

transitions.title: The dominant releases a string melody
transitions.how: The renewed horn-call preparation diminishes onto a held G-dominant harmony. Out of that space, violins introduce the broad C-major tune over plucked cellos and basses, with horns supporting rather than overwhelming the melody. The change to Allegro non troppo, ma con brio gives the long phrase a new forward pace. Its melodic outline has already been anticipated in the darker opening.
transitions.evidence: The first-edition score p. 52 begins the Allegro at bar 62. The report’s internal minimum at 4:30 and boundary at 4:34 anchor the approximate 274-second change; instrument identities are score-derived.

transitions.title: Recognition begins another development
transitions.how: The exposition’s E-minor closing gestures give way to quiet rising figures in the winds. The broad main tune returns in C major with fuller accompaniment, but its continuation turns towards E♭ rather than remaining at home. Brahms combines returning themes with further development: the tune is recognisable before its surrounding harmonies are settled.
transitions.evidence: Bars 176–186 link the exposition’s cadence to the returning main theme. The report drops at 8:20, recovers at 8:25 and subsequently changes tonal region around 8:55–9:00. The 505-second return is a score-proportional estimate.

transitions.title: The returning call prepares another theme
transitions.how: The later return of the horn melody does not simply recreate its earlier route into the main tune. Its continuation broadens and withdraws, leading instead to the second group. The familiar four-note descent now belongs to C-major surroundings, alternating between winds and lower strings. The return is therefore both tonal and orchestral: a bass pattern recovers its function in a changed distribution of parts.
transitions.evidence: Bars 289–301 carry the horn melody into the returning second group. The report falls through 12:30–12:50 and changes at 12:54, supporting the 774-second anchor; no individual calando or solo entry is precisely aligned.

transitions.title: Quiet fragments prepare the expanded chorale
transitions.how: The later C-minor closing group withdraws into quiet fragments of the main theme, including low-brass and lower-string recollection. Tremolo and a timpani roll support an accelerating buildup. Più allegro then turns decisively towards C major, and the chorale from the introduction returns with enlarged orchestral force. The closing span therefore changes pace and weight without needing an unrelated final theme.
transitions.evidence: Bars 367–390 prepare the coda; bar 391 marks Più allegro and bar 407 the chorale. The report’s 14:48 boundary begins the quieter preparation before the sustained rise at 15:05–15:30. Only the start of this combined closing span is mapped.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: Movement IV, pp. 43–100. Opening, Più andante (p. 48), chorale (p. 50, bars 47–51) and Allegro (p. 52) inspected directly; later representative textures follow Hansen’s bar descriptions. Entries are approximate passage snapshots, not continuous instrument tracking or an ear-checked alignment.

timeline.note: Low-string descent and the slow upper phrase establish the Adagio’s sustained texture.
All-string pizzicato figures pass between registers in the first accelerating interruption.
The Più andante introduces the horn call over quiet brass support, timpani and muted string tremolo.
The flute carries the call through its later introductory statement over the continuing string background.
Trombones and bassoons present the compact chorale with contrabassoon and lower-horn support; isolated plucked string chords punctuate it before the horn-call preparation resumes.
The broad Allegro tune begins in strings over plucked lower strings and supporting horns.
Expanded orchestration turns fragments of the main melody into transition material.
The second group sets its melodic line above the recurring four-note bass descent.
The broad tune returns with richer wind punctuation and horn support before further development.
The later horn-call region uses smoother moving strings rather than the introduction’s tremolo background.
The later second group redistributes its descending bass figure between low strings and winds.
The final preparation recalls main-theme fragments in low brass and lower strings beneath a growing upper texture.
The coda expands the introductory chorale into a full-orchestral statement.

composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
facts: Piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Seasonal work in Detmold, 1857–59; Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64; Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde concerts, 1872–75
Based in Vienna; summer composition in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano music, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.
